item.title: [MLB.com] Rays-Yankees ALDS Game 3 FAQ (Wed., 8 p.m. ET, TBS/HBO Max)
item.dc:creator: Adam Berry; Bryan Hoch
item.description: NEW YORK -- Two weeks ago, the Rays went wild in the visitors’ clubhouse at Yankee Stadium after clinching their first American League East championship in five years. That party started shortly after a win over the Yankees and carried late into the New York night. Could they have another celebration in store in the Bronx? It’s time for the American League Division Series to shift venues, going from the Rays’ home dome at Tropicana Field to Yankee Stadium for Game 3 on Wednesday night. But the R
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- Two weeks ago, the Rays went wild in the visitors’ clubhouse at Yankee Stadium after clinching their first American League East championship in five years. That party started shortly after a win over the Yankees and carried late into the New York night.
Could they have another celebration in store in the Bronx?
It’s time for the American League Division Series to shift venues, going from the Rays’ home dome at Tropicana Field to Yankee Stadium for Game 3 on Wednesday night. But the Rays are still right where they want to be, holding a commanding 2-0 lead in the series with three chances to advance to the AL Championship Series.
“It's amazing, man. It's exactly the way we wanted to start the series,” Rays closer Bryan Baker said. “To be able to play in front of these fans in this building and take a 2-0 series lead was exactly what we wanted, so it feels really good right now.”
Maybe home-field advantage is what the Yankees need after coming up empty against Rays ace Drew Rasmussen in Game 1 and kicking the ball around the infield in a mistake-filled Game 2 defeat. Or maybe it’ll help to send left-hander Max Fried to the mound, knowing how tough he’s been on Tampa Bay throughout his career.
“We've got to get over it,” Yankees manager Aaron Boone said after Game 2. “We've responded all year to difficult times, and we've got to do that again. We've got to get ourselves up off the mat.”
Tampa Bay’s pitching staff held what looked like a red-hot New York lineup to only two runs in the first 18 innings of this series. If the Rays keep that up, they could enjoy another champagne-soaked night in the city that never sleeps.
“I think it's sweet either way. Doesn't matter the clubhouse,” Rays center fielder Jonny DeLuca said. “Obviously, going over there, having the chance to do that would be pretty special.”
When is the game and how can I watch it?
First pitch for Game 3 of the Yankees-Rays Division Series is set for 8 p.m. ET on Wednesday at Yankee Stadium. The game will be broadcast on TBS, truTV and HBO Max.
The ALDS will be available in Spanish on UniMas, while Univision’s TUDN Radio will provide Spanish-language audio coverage. ESPN Radio will provide live national coverage of all 2026 MLB Postseason games.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Rays: Nick Martinez, RHP
Key stats: 7-3, 2.38 ERA in 16 road starts this season
After rolling out Rasmussen in Game 1 and Freddy Peralta in Game 2, Martinez was the logical choice for the Rays with the series moving to the Bronx. The veteran right-hander was a reliable presence on the mound for Tampa Bay all season, as he posted a 3.10 ERA over 180 innings while the club went 22-9 in his starts. He was at his best on the road, including two outings in the Bronx. The first-time All-Star held the Yankees to only three runs over 12 innings in their home ballpark.
Yankees: Max Fried, LHP
Key stats: 5-1, 1.81 ERA in 7 career GS vs. Tampa Bay
Fried is coming off a sharp outing against the Red Sox in the decisive Game 2 of the AL Wild Card Series, holding Boston to a run on three hits over six innings. Fried walked one and struck out six, his third postseason start since joining the Yankees.
This will be Fried’s third time facing the Rays this season. He last saw them on Sept. 22 in New York, taking the loss in a 6 2/3-inning effort as Tampa Bay clinched the AL East.
Fried also went up against the Rays on April 11 at Tropicana Field, taking a no-decision after permitting three runs over eight innings. For his career, Fried is 5-1 with a 1.81 ERA in seven starts vs. Tampa Bay, including 3-0 with a 0.84 ERA in three starts during the 2025 season.
What might the starting lineups look like?
Rays: It seems likely the Rays will change things up a bit against the Yankees’ left-handers, opting for the right-handed side of most platoons and leaving their lefty hitters available off the bench. Here’s one potential look for a more right-handed lineup.
Yankees: The Yankees have used the same lefty-heavy lineup three times this postseason against right-handed pitchers, including twice in the ALDS. Boone said he is considering shaking things up for Game 3. Boone said before Game 2 that he was considering starting Anthony Volpe at third base. Jose Caballero and Paul Goldschmidt could also enter the mix.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Rays: The Rays really couldn’t be in much better shape thanks to their starting rotation. Rasmussen handled eight innings in Game 1, and the duo of Peralta and Ian Seymour combined to work 7 2/3 innings in Game 2. So, their traditional relievers have recorded seven of the 54 outs so far this series: six from Baker and a big one from lefty Cam Booser. They may not turn to Peralta or Seymour in Game 3, but they still have starter Griffin Jax available -- and the Yankees have yet to face setup men Tyler Wells and Kevin Kelly in this series.
Yankees: Ryan Weathers replaced infielder/outfielder Amed Rosario for this series, returning from a left flexor strain sustained in late August. David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick should all be leaned upon for high-leverage outs. Will Warren is now in the bullpen after appearing in 32 games (29 starts) during the regular season. Warren made one appearance in the Wild Card Series, tossing 1 2/3 innings.
Any injuries of note?
Rays: Nothing new. Everyone who was expected to be available for this series is on the roster. The most notable injury situation to watch moving forward is that of left-hander Shane McClanahan, whose status is unclear except that he will not pitch in this series.
Yankees: Aaron Judge was left off the ALDS roster, though Boone said it was a “close” call. Judge has yet to run the bases as he recovers from a right calf strain, though he has been performing outfield running. He has also been taking numerous live at-bats while throwing. Clarke Schmidt has been ruled out for the remainder of the postseason.
Who is hot and who is not?
Rays: Aranda doesn’t get as much love as the other members of the “Big Three,” but his left-handed bat is key. He hit better than either Caminero or Díaz in September, and he had the lone big hit of the night in Game 1 before picking up two more hits in Game 2. Richie Palacios finished strong, too, posting a .981 OPS with five homers in September before delivering the biggest hit of Game 2, and the Brooklyn native likes hitting against his hometown Yankees. Tampa Bay’s entire rotation surged into the postseason, highlighted by Rasmussen and Peralta, the September AL Pitcher of the Month.
The Rays’ outfield is off to a slow start in this series, offensively, but they all showed the impact they can have by putting the ball in play in Game 2. And their defense has been consistently excellent.
Yankees: Rice has been the Yankees' most productive hitter in the postseason, and given how the ALDS has gone, it hasn't been particularly close. Rice is 7-for-15 (.467) in the playoffs, including his two-homer performance in ALDS Game 2. Rice has four homers and eight RBIs overall. Wells is 5-for-12 (.417) in the playoffs, including a couple of doubles in the ALDS. Everyone except for Rice and Wells has combined to go 1-for-46 (.022) in the ALDS so far.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• The Yankees won four of the six games these clubs played in the Bronx during the regular season, splitting a pair of games in late May, then taking three of four the final week of the season. However, the Rays have already celebrated once at Yankee Stadium, as they clinched the AL East title with a 6-1 win in the second half of a doubleheader on Sept. 22.

item.title: [BoSox Injection] MLB silently confirms Yankees fans whining about Sonny Gray cheating were wasting their time
item.dc:creator: Katie Manganelli
item.description: Sonny Gray pitched a great game against the New York Yankees in Wild Card Game 2. Chad Tracy pulled him in the fifth inning despite the single run he'd allowed at that point and the Boston Red Sox crumbled from there. During the game, some fans noticed some brown flecks on the right side of Gray's neck, on the same side as his pitching arm. Speculation about cheating ran rampant on social media despite the veteran passing all his in-game hand and glove checks from the umpires. Chris Cotillo on O
item.content:encoded:
Sonny Gray pitched a great game against the New York Yankees in Wild Card Game 2. Chad Tracy pulled him in the fifth inning despite the single run he'd allowed at that point and the Boston Red Sox crumbled from there.
During the game, some fans noticed some brown flecks on the right side of Gray's neck, on the same side as his pitching arm. Speculation about cheating ran rampant on social media despite the veteran passing all his in-game hand and glove checks from the umpires.
Chris Cotillo on October 6 reported that MLB investigated Gray for the potential use of illegal substances. Since Gray has not been officially disciplined by the league and he passed all the in-game examinations, Cotillo assumes he's in the clear.
While it was evident that Gray had something on his neck, it didn't look like pine tar, which can be seen in dark, glossy layers on players' helmets and bats. in April 2024, Yankees pitcher Michael Pineda was ejected for using pine tar, which he rubbed on his neck before the game, to improve his grip on the ball. The pine tar was in a uniform smear on his neck and not pilled up, as whatever was on Gray's neck appeared.
MLB investigated Red Sox's Sonny Gray for rumors of illegal sticky substance use in Wild Card Game 2 against Yankees
If there was something sticky on Gray's neck that remained there after he rubbed his fingers over it before nearly every batter, it would remain on his hands when he presented them to umpires to be checked after every inning.
It wasn't even unique for Gray to touch his neck before every pitch — he's been seen doing the same swiping motion on the side of his neck countless times. Using sweat to increase the stickiness of rosin on one's hands, a completely legal substance, is a trick used by pitchers throughout the league over many years.
Gray was the Sox's ace all season and he gave his teammates a great start in the postseason without cheating. His 2.72 ERA over 169 innings this season and 1.98 ERA in two starts against the Yankees aren't indicative of someone who needs extra, illegal help to get through games.
Gray is an impending free agent and the Sox's 2027 rotation will miss him dearly. He was the only righty in the rotation and his 18 wins matched Garrett Crochet's total in 2025. Both pitchers were incredibly effective stoppers in their full seasons with Boston.
Gray's tenure with the Red Sox didn't end on the best note, as he was dissatisfied with Tracy's decision to pull him so early in the game. But if Boston seeks a reunion with Gray, it can do so in good conscience, knowing he didn't use illegal substances in a playoff game.

item.title: [roundtable.io] How White Sox Turned ‘Organized Chaos’ Into a Postseason Weapon
item.dc:creator: Sam Phalen
item.description: Chicago's unconventional pitching plan has dominated October, but its postseason success was built through a full season of preparation. Now just one win away from advancing to the ALCS, it's becoming undeniable that this group has a little bit of magic to it. These White Sox are young, hungry, and they don't know what they don't know. They show up to the ballpark every day believing they can win. And sometimes in the postseason, that spirit is enough to carry a team. Baseball, however, isn't ju
item.content:encoded:
Chicago's unconventional pitching plan has dominated October, but its postseason success was built through a full season of preparation.
Now just one win away from advancing to the ALCS, it's becoming undeniable that this group has a little bit of magic to it. These White Sox are young, hungry, and they don't know what they don't know.
They show up to the ballpark every day believing they can win. And sometimes in the postseason, that spirit is enough to carry a team.
Baseball, however, isn't just watching Chicago with admiration for the Cinderella story at hand. There's also a somewhat unprecedented strategy being deployed by the White Sox this October, one that could change the way teams shape their pitching staffs moving forward if this level of success continues.
Organized chaos.
That's what the White Sox call their pitching strategy for the postseason.
Right-hander Sean Burke is the only truly reliable traditional starting pitcher the White Sox have on their playoff roster. So Chicago has largely thrown standard pitching roles out the window. Manager Will Venable plays the matchups on a nearly pitch-by-pitch basis, deploying an all-hands-on-deck approach to cover the 27 outs necessary for victory.
Unconventional? Absolutely. But it's also been remarkably effective.
Even Burke hasn't been used as a traditional starting pitcher. And why would he be?
Burke entered Monday's ALDS Game 2 against the Cleveland Guardians in the third inning after Chicago used two openers to begin the game. The White Sox wanted to roll out a pair of left-handers, Anthony Kay and Sean Newcomb, to navigate the top of Cleveland's lineup and neutralize its dangerous left-handed bats before turning things over to Burke.
The strategy also shortened the game for Burke, allowing him to attack hitters without worrying about pacing himself for a traditional six- or seven-inning start.
He was lights out.
Burke pitched into the bottom of the eighth inning and likely could have kept going. At one point, he set a franchise postseason record with 13 consecutive batters retired. Then with the White Sox nursing a 4-2 lead, Venable ultimately decided there was no reason to push it.
The White Sox have now allowed just nine total runs over four postseason games while pitching to a 1.75 team ERA.
All anybody wants to know is how they've managed to make it work. After all, it's not like the White Sox had an incredible pitching staff throughout the regular season. Their 4.12 team ERA was right around the MLB average.
Not to mention, this is an incredibly young White Sox team with plenty of young arms. Many of them are getting their first taste of playoff baseball during this current run. And inexperienced pitchers are usually expected to show some signs of fatigue this late in the season as they blow past previous career highs in innings pitched.
Instead, the opposite has happened. The deeper the White Sox have gotten into the season, the more dominant their pitching staff has become.
So why is it working for Chicago?
Because the White Sox put it into practice during the regular season.
Consistency has been a primary focus for Venable as he takes this young team into the postseason. He wants players in the same positions, doing things they're familiar with. His message in pregame speeches hasn't changed. And when it comes to the pitching staff, they're comfortable being used as Swiss Army knives because that's how they've been deployed all year.
Instead, Chicago learned how to survive without one.
Using an opener in front of a starting pitcher, throwing a bullpen game, asking relievers to cover multiple innings. These are all things the White Sox did during the regular season to get themselves into the playoffs.
Nothing about what Venable is asking his pitchers to do in October is foreign to them. The stakes are higher and the margin for error is smaller, but the roles themselves haven't suddenly changed.
"Organized chaos" from the pitching staff was a necessity for the White Sox to survive 162 games. Now it's becoming a weapon in the postseason.
The young right-hander admitted Chicago's original plan for the game went a bit haywire after Cleveland scored two runs in the first inning, forcing Venable to make an earlier-than-expected move to the bullpen for Newcomb.
But Burke was prepared for the unconventional situation, in part because he leaned on teammates who had already experienced similar roles.
He specifically mentioned Erick Fedde, Sean Newcomb and White Sox bullpen coach Matt Wise as people he leaned on while establishing a routine and rhythm for entering a game after it had already started.
It's another example of why Chicago's organized chaos works. The White Sox aren't improvising in October. They're leaning on the versatility, preparation and experience they spent an entire season developing. Keeping things consistent is an underrated aspect of playoff baseball.
For many teams, the bright lights of October make them tighten up. There's a misconception that you need to play differently and treat these games differently simply because they mean more.
And yes, fundamentally sound baseball becomes increasingly important when the margin for error shrinks. But the White Sox are showing how familiarity, comfort and playing loose can actually be the key to postseason success.
That includes the unconventional approach to team pitching.
It doesn't matter if you're a starter or reliever. It doesn't matter if you're being asked to pitch five innings or throw five pitches. The goal is the same: Get 27 outs.
Guys like Burke are flexible enough to make it work. Venable has continued pushing all the right buttons. And the White Sox have built a pitching staff that's comfortable operating without the traditional roles that have defined the sport for generations.
It started as a necessity during the regular season. It's become one of Chicago's greatest strengths in October.
And if this White Sox playoff run continues, don't be surprised if more teams around Major League Baseball start trying to replicate it.

item.content:encoded:
By splitting the first two games of the National League Division Series, Atlanta essentially turned a five-game series into a three-game series -- and, oh, by the way, stole home-field advantage from the Dodgers in the process.
Next up, each team will turn to its respective staff ace in a pivotal Game 3 as the series shifts to Truist Park on Tuesday night.
“We know it's two good teams going at it,” Dodgers first baseman Freddie Freeman said. “We know what's at stake on Tuesday. We need to get that win.”
Just how badly does each team need that win? Consider this: In postseason history, the Game 3 winner in a best-of-five series tied 1-1 has gone on to win the series 48 of 67 times (71.6%).
Here’s everything you need to know ahead of the crucial Game 3:
When is the game and how can I watch it?
First pitch for Game 3 is set for 6 p.m. ET/3 p.m. PT on Tuesday at Truist Park. It will be broadcast on FS1/FOX Deportes/FOX One.
All series are available in the US on MLB.TV with authentication to a participating Pay TV provider. Games are also available live internationally, although not in Canada. Sportsnet is MLB's exclusive English-language broadcaster in Canada for every Postseason game, while TVA Sports will be covering the entire AL Postseason and the World Series in French and Broadcaster RDS will cover the entire NL Postseason in French.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Dodgers: RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto   
Key stat: 0.87 WHIP, ranked second among qualified MLB starters
The reigning World Series MVP is set for his 2026 postseason debut with his team looking to reclaim its series lead. Yamamoto could have started Game 1, but the Dodgers liked the way they were lined up for the NLDS and beyond with Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell starting the first two contests. L.A.'s ace is up third as the series shifts to Atlanta, where he gave up one run across 6 1/3 strong innings on Aug. 27; he was outdueled by Sale in a 1-0 loss.
Braves: LHP Chris Sale   
Key stat:  1.96 ERA over his final 24 regular-season starts
Sale will face the Dodgers for the first time since throwing a five-hit shutout against them on Aug. 27. The 37-year-old posted MLB’s third-best ERA (2.16) this year. He began the postseason by limiting the Phillies to three runs over 6 1/3 innings in Game 1 of the NL Wild Card Series. There was some thought about having him start Game 2, but because he recorded the final four outs of Game 3 of the WC Series, the Braves pushed him back.
What are the starting lineups?
Dodgers: The big change for LA's Game 3 lineup is Shohei Ohtani in the No. 5 spot. Until Tuesday, Ohtani, recovering from right biceps and left knee injuries, had not been fifth or lower in a starting lineup since Sept. 23, 2020. With Sale on the mound, the Dodgers are not only stacking the top half of their lineup mostly with right-handed hitters, they're shaking up their typical starting nine. They already started Miguel Rojas at third base over Max Muncy when facing a lefty opener in Game 2, so it's not a surprise to see Kiké Hernández getting his first start this postseason at the hot corner, shifting Rojas to second.
Braves: Drake Baldwin’s leadoff homer accounted for the game’s only run the last time the Braves faced Yamamoto. Baldwin, Matt Olson and Michael Harris II should all enjoy seeing a right-handed starter. The Braves had faced a lefty starter in four of their first five postseason games. Aaron Nola, the only right-hander they’ve seen, lasted just 1 2/3 innings in Game 3 of the NLWC Series.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Braves: Coming off an off-day, the Braves will have closer Raisel Iglesias and two top setup men, Robert Suarez and Dylan Lee, available. Didier Fuentes and Ray Kerr won’t be available after both threw 40-plus pitches on Sunday.
Dodgers: The bullpen had to cover the final 5 1/3 innings of Game 2 after a shaky start from Snell, but after a series off-day, the Dodgers should have almost everyone available for Game 3. The exception may be Roki Sasaki, who threw two innings on 36 pitches on Sunday.
Any injuries of note?
Dodgers: Ohtani (right biceps, left knee) and Freeman (right knee) are managing lingering injuries. World Series hero Will Klein (right elbow discomfort) has faced hitters, but he has not pitched in a game since July 31 and is viewed as more of a depth option. Blake Treinen (right shoulder inflammation) is unlikely to pitch this postseason.
Who is hot and who is not?
Braves: Harris has two three-hit efforts in five games this postseason and is 8-for-20 (.400) overall. The Braves hope to get Acuña (3-for-18 without an extra-base hit) and Olson (3-for-19 with seven strikeouts) going as the series goes on.
Dodgers: After a tough September, Freeman (3-for-7, home run) swung the bat well in the first two games. Pages (0-for-7) and Tommy Edman (0-for-5) are seeking their first hits this postseason.
Anything else fans might want to know?
- This will be the first time Sale has faced the Dodgers in the postseason since coming out of the Red Sox bullpen to pitch a perfect ninth inning to conclude the 2018 World Series.
- Roberts enters Game 3 one win shy of 71 managerial postseason wins, which would tie Tony La Russa for second-most all-time. Joe Torre holds the record with 84.

item.dc:creator: Caleb Kerney
item.description: The Atlanta Braves have an opportunity to break the 1-1 tie and take the lead in their NLDS series against the reigning MLB World Series Champions. Prior to taking on the Los Angeles Dodgers, the Braves announced news about Ha-Seong Kim. Game 3 features a pitching matchup for the ages. Game 3 will start at 4:00 PM Mountain Time, 3:00 PM Pacific Time, or 6:00 P
item.content:encoded:
The Atlanta Braves have an opportunity to break the 1-1 tie and take the lead in their NLDS series against the reigning MLB World Series Champions. Prior to taking on the Los Angeles Dodgers, the Braves announced news about Ha-Seong Kim.
Game 3 features a pitching matchup for the ages. Chris Sale takes the mound for the Braves, fresh off a 3-2 win that evened the series. Yoshinobu Yamamoto is the starter for the Dodgers.
Game 3 will start at 4:00 PM Mountain Time, 3:00 PM Pacific Time, or 6:00 PM Eastern Time.
Atlanta Braves Announce Ha-Seong Kim & Lane Thomas News Before NLDS Game 3 vs. the Los Angeles Dodgers
Before the first pitch of Game 3 in the NLDS between the Braves and Dodgers, the Braves announced news regarding Kim. This announcement is in regard to his placement in the lineup for the game.
Here is the lineup that the Braves announced prior to the game:
- C: Drake Baldwin
- RF: Ronald Acuna Jr.
- 1B: Matt Olson
- 2B: Ozzie Albies
- CF: Michael Harris II
- LF: Mauricio Dubon
- DH: Sean Murphy
- 3B: Austin Riley
- SS: Ha-Seong Kim
Starting Pitcher: Chris Sale
As you can see, the Braves are going with a near-identical lineup for Game 3. However, the biggest change is pulling Lane Thomas and inserting Kim.
After that, the only other change is moving Dubon from shortstop to LF (to cover the removed Thomas).
Kim is a 30-year-old infielder who played 51 regular-season games. Thomas is a 31-year-old outfielder who came over to the Braves in a trade with the Kansas City Royals at the trade deadline.
Reaction To Atlanta Braves Game 3 Lineup
MLB insider Mark Bowman tried to explain today’s lineup decisions.
“Rowdy isn’t in today’s lineup. This weekend, Walt said he likes to have Murphy at DH and Baldwin at C because it allows him to PH for Murph at the right point of a game,” Bowman wrote.
A curious fan brought up an argument, and Bowman responded.
“But why wouldn’t he stack as many LHH as possible in the starting lineup against a tough righty? Could have gone Dubon at SS, Yaz in LF, Tellez at DH…..” the fan wrote.
Bowman replied with some stats regarding Yamamoto: “Yamamoto vs. RHH .586 OPS vs. LHH .510 OPS.”
Looking At Ha-Seong Kim & Lane Thomas
Kim has yet to find success during this postseason run.
Despite playing three games and earning four at-bats, he has yet to record a hit. However, he has recorded a single run, thanks to one of his two walks.
During the regular season, Kim had more offensive success.
In his 51 games, Kim recorded 15 hits, one double, one triple, nine RBIs, 16 walks, and two stolen bases to go along with a .116 batting average.
Thomas, on the other hand, hasn’t experienced much more success than Kim. He has 73 hits, 19 doubles, 40 RBIs, 44 walks, nine stolen bases, and 11 home runs in 118 games.
Additionally, he has a .224 batting average.
It looks like this change could simply be to give Thomas a night off and make sure that Kim gets a game. Because if the Braves were trying to make sure everyone in the lineup could contribute offensively, this is a strange choice.
One way or another, the Braves need to get a win to turn the tides in their favor and take a lead in the series before Game 4.

item.content:encoded:
The scenes shift for Game 3 of the National League Division Series on Tuesday, Oct. 6, and prediction markets offer great trading opportunities.
Unpredictable things happen during the MLB postseason, but if you think you know what will happen, you can stake your claim on Kalshi and Polymarket US.
Aces Chris Sale and Yoshinobu Yamamoto will square off at Atlanta’s Truist Park in a star-studded pitching matchup between the Braves and two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers. The series is even at 1 after Atlanta’s 3-2 win at Dodger Stadium in Game 2.
The Milwaukee Brewers will try to sweep the San Diego Padres in the nightcap at San Diego’s Petco Park.
Let’s look closer at the best sports prediction markets and prices for today’s two games.
Best MLB props for National League Playoffs today
LA Dodgers at Atlanta Braves over/under market
Why Over 6.5 runs could hit
Probability: 51% at Kalshi
Sale and Yamamoto are aces, but these are two of baseball’s most prolific offenses. The Dodgers, of course, have MVPs batting Nos. 1-3 (Mookie Betts, Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman), and Freeman is heating up after an ice-cold September.
Seven runs isn’t a high bar to clear, especially considering Sale’s struggles in October. Sale has a 5.83 ERA in 12 career postseason appearances and allowed three runs to the Phillies in his last postseason start.
The teams totaled eight runs in Game 1, which Dodgers star Tarik Skubal started.
Why Under 6.5 runs could hit
Probability: 49% at ProphetX
These are two of the best pitchers in baseball, and Yamamoto specifically has been a big-game pitcher since he came over from Japan. He was the 2025 World Series MVP. Fewer than seven runs were scored in five of his nine career postseason starts.
Sale has been a bulldog throughout his career, and he’ll need to rise to the occasion to match Yamamoto in an enormous game.
Even though these offenses have elite players, they have not gotten unlocked. Braves star outfielder Ronald Acuna Jr. has a .485 postseason OPS, and Matt Olsen’s is .543. On the Dodgers’ side, Ohtani, Betts and Will Smith have combined for three hits in 21 at-bats.
Those numbers don’t bode well when facing aces. The first team to two runs may win Game 3.
Milwaukee Brewers at San Diego Padres first five innings market
Why the Padres could win the first five innings
Probability: 47% at Polymarket
The Padres have been striking early throughout the postseason. They have scored first in all four games and have held 2-0 leads in each game in this series.
The Padres have been one of the most dominant teams at home this year, too. They went 51-30 at Petco Park during the regular season and had no trouble rolling the Cubs in the Wild Card round.
Plus, Dustin May is by far the Brewers’ shakiest starting pitcher. He has good career numbers against the Padres (3.14 ERA in 86 innings) but also may be nervous since this will be his first postseason appearance in six years.
Why the Brewers could win the first five innings
Probability: 37% at Kalshi
Milwaukee’s offense has been slow to get going in the series, but it can keep the momentum after its emotional win over the Padres and closer Mason Miller in Game 2.
May may not get more than three innings, but the Brewers bullpen has been awesome, especially in this series. Milwaukee has not allowed any runs in nine innings.
If May can hold down San Diego for one turn through the order, the Brewers can win the first five innings and Game 3.
How prediction markets work for MLB Playoffs trading
All prediction market trades are peer-to-peer, meaning you need a fellow user to buy and sell shares.
Users buy ‘Yes’ and ‘No’ shares on sports results. Each share costs $0.01 to $0.99. All winning shares pay out $1. Losing shares pay out nothing. Low share prices produce bigger payouts.
You can use prediction markets like a sportsbook and wait for your game to finish, or you can use them like the registered financial exchanges they are. If you choose the latter, you can day trade outcomes by buying shares at a low price and selling higher for incremental profit.
Of course, there is risk with any way you trade on sports. Luckily, you can earn valuable site credit by claiming new-user bonuses with the top prediction market promos.

item.dc:creator: Adam Burke
item.description: MLB Best Bets Today October 6 The AL steps aside and the NL takes center stage, as we get Game 3s with a change of scenery in Dodgers vs. Braves and Brewers vs. Padres. item.content:encoded:
MLB Best Bets Today October 6
The AL steps aside and the NL takes center stage, as we get Game 3s with a change of scenery in Dodgers vs. Braves and Brewers vs. Padres. After a long day of travel, the teams are back at it, as San Diego looks to stave off elimination and LA and Atlanta are both searching for a huge win to take control of the series. That game has Yoshinobu Yamamoto vs. Chris Sale, while the other game has the potential for all kinds of craziness and lots of bullpen arms. Two very different games to say the least.
Throughout the playoffs, I’ll look at every game on the schedule, even if I don’t have any bets. I’ll typically do this on the morning of the games, trying to achieve as much lead time as possible. Bullpen usage is critically important in the postseason, so I’d be doing a major disservice to do anything before the games are finished and that usually means writing up my thoughts in the morning.
All lines are from DraftKings and are current at the time of publish. Please take the initiative to SHOP AROUND for the best odds. It matters. A lot.
One offering this baseball season is our Opta AI Player Prop Projections. They are for VSiN Pro Subscribers only, so you can check out our current offers here.
Feel free to use my opinions and thoughts, as well as our suite of MLB Betting Tools, including the DraftKings and Circa Betting Splits, Steve Makinen’s Daily Ratings, the 1st 5 Innings Analyzer, and Umpire Stats.
Here are the MLB best bets today for October 6:
Dodgers vs. Braves (-110, 6)
6 p.m. ET
The Dodgers and Braves have flipped back and forth as ever so slight favorites in what is basically a coin-flip affair in Atlanta. The total of 6 definitely illustrates the quality of this pitching matchup, especially because of the caliber of the players in these two lineups. Obviously the Dodgers were among the league’s best and the Braves, while very talented, had a lot of inconsistencies with their hitters.
Sale finished the regular season with a 2.16 ERA, 2.97 xERA, and a 2.29 FIP over his 162.2 innings of work. So far this postseason, he’s pitched 7.2 innings with one start and one relief effort, allowing three runs on five hits with a 12/2 K/BB ratio. Some will probably point to his poor postseason numbers with a 5.83 ERA over 41.2 innings of work, but this is his first time back in the playoffs since 2021, so I’m not really sure any of that matters for what he is now.
LA was fifth in wOBA at .331 against LHP during the regular season, though not all lefties are created equal and not many are Sale. If we start cutting down the sample size, the Dodgers were seventh in wOBA at .329 in the second half against lefties and second with a .366 wOBA in the month of September. But, their 13% BB% is not applicable against a guy like Sale, who throws a lot of strikes.
I’m a bit surprised that the Dodgers didn’t roll with Yamamoto in Game 2, opting instead for Blake Snell. Yamamoto had a 2.53 ERA with a 2.94 xERA and a 3.33 FIP during the regular season over 185 innings. He also would have broken up the run of two straight lefties, but Dave Roberts acknowledged that the Dodgers were thinking about their rotation with the NLCS already, which is pretty presumptuous and was probably some bulletin board material for the Braves.
Yamamoto has already thrown 56 postseason innings with a 2.25 ERA and a 3.45 FIP, as his K% hasn’t been as high, but his BB% has been even better. The Braves were 11th in the league with a .319 wOBA against righties. They were definitely worse against lefties, which perhaps had something to do with Snell being the Game 2 call. The Braves had .316 wOBA against RHP in the second half and had a .317 wOBA against them in September.
Sale has only allowed more than three runs in one start this season, which happened back on April 6. Yamamoto allowed four runs in two of his four September starts. This is a very tight game to say the least. I don’t like a pregame bet in this one. I don’t even have a line on side or total.
Brewers vs. Padres (-138, 7.5)
9:30 p.m. ET
Dustin May and Nick Pivetta are the listed starters here, as this is a much different game than the other one. I’m actually not expecting to see May for very long. I think the right-hander is going to get the team through Fernando Tatis, Manny Machado, and Ty France at least once and maybe try to navigate the bottom of the lineup. My expectation is that we see both Robert Gasser and Shane Drohan. Maybe even Kyle Harrison. There is a lot of data out there about teams hitting relievers better the more that they see them. Those three and Chad Patrick have not pitched yet in this series.
Meanwhile, Trevor Megill, Abner Uribe, and Aaron Ashby have all pitched in both games, while Antonio Senzatela, JoJo Romero, and DL Hall each have one appearance. This will be an all hands on deck approach from Milwaukee and I wouldn’t be surprised if the Padres hitters see a different arm in each plate appearance. May in a short burst sitting 98-99 with movement might fare a bit better than what he usually does.
On the San Diego side, Pivetta really struggled his way through 3.1 innings against the Cubs with four strikeouts and two walks. He only gave up one run on three hits, but it was an arduous appearance. Pivetta only made eight starts during the regular season, with four to start the season and four to finish it. He only allowed 11 runs over 34.2 innings when all was said and done and just three runs in his final four starts.
Joe Musgrove and David Morgan have not pitched in this series yet. Yuki Matsui and Bradgley Rodriguez worked back-to-back days in Games 1 and 2. Mason Miller threw 40 pitches with the loss in Game 2 and Adrian Morejon threw 31 with the loss in Game 1. We could see Walker Buehler here as well as Robbie Ray.
I like the setup better for Milwaukee here with a cavalcade of arms, including several lefties that they can deploy if they wish. I don’t think May will factor into the game as much as the line implies. More specialists for Milwaukee can pitch in the middle innings and guys who can give the Friars a different look. As the underdog price, I think the Brewers are worth a look tonight.
Pick: Brewers +114

item.dc:creator: Ben Clemens
item.description: When I’m trying to ground myself in the present, I like to repeat a mantra: No past, no future. I don’t want to dictate personal philosophy to you, but it works great for me. It’s a reminder to focus on the now, that experiencing what’s happening right this instant is more important than whatever mental baggage I’m carrying or whatever I’m worried might take place next week. item.content:encoded:
When I’m trying to ground myself in the present, I like to repeat a mantra: No past, no future. I don’t want to dictate personal philosophy to you, but it works great for me. It’s a reminder to focus on the now, that experiencing what’s happening right this instant is more important than whatever mental baggage I’m carrying or whatever I’m worried might take place next week. I wholeheartedly suggest some variation of this phrase when you’re feeling overwhelmed by things that aren’t happening to you in the moment.
Having said that, let me be clear: You can’t ignore the past and future when you’re managing postseason pitching assignments, Walt Weiss. The Braves are five games into the playoffs, and they’ve been living the “no past, no future” life the entire time. Now, I actually think that has some useful consequences. The present really does matter quite a bit in playoff baseball – more than the future, and certainly more than the past. But it’s also caused them plenty of problems. The clearest example is also the most notable move Weiss has made so far. The Braves deployed bullpen games in each of the first two games of the NLDS over the weekend. The first was unavoidable, a consequence of their injury-depleted rotation, but the second was the direct consequence of Weiss’ earlier actions.
I’m talking about Chris Sale, of course. Sale started the Wild Card opener against the Phillies last Tuesday and worked into the seventh, throwing 95 pitches before departing with two on, one out, and the bottom of the Philly lineup coming to the plate. After a little turbulence (Didier Fuentes allowed both inherited runners to score, giving the Phillies the lead), the Braves pulled it out. But after Philadelphia won the second game of the series, Weiss called on Sale to cover the final four outs of the decisive Game 3.
Ben is a writer at FanGraphs. He can be found on Bluesky @benclemens.

This is still a roster
item.content:encoded:
2 trades Astros must make this offseason after early postseason exit appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Houston Astros cannot react to an early postseason exit with minor roster adjustments. After finishing 81-81 and getting swept by the Chicago White Sox in the American League Wild Card Series, Houston needs to attack its two weaknesses: its rotation and an offense lacking speed and dependable outfield production.
This is still a roster built to compete around Yordan Alvarez, Jose Altuve, Carlos Correa, Jeremy Peña and Hunter Brown. However, the Astros need more than a depth starter and a platoon outfielder if they intend to make another serious run in 2027.
Houston should pursue two aggressive trades. Neither would be inexpensive, but both would address a major weakness without forcing the organization into a rebuild.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Trade for Mariners ace Logan Gilbert
Astros receive: RHP Logan Gilbert
Mariners receive: INF Xavier Neyens, RHP Ethan Pecko and OF Joseph Sullivan
Trading within the AL West would create an obvious obstacle, but Houston should still call Seattle about Gilbert. The 29-year-old is entering his final year before free agency, making him a logical trade candidate if the Mariners do not believe they can sign him to an extension.
Gilbert would give the Astros the durable frontline starter they lacked throughout 2026. He finished the season with a 12-11 record, 3.73 ERA, 1.09 WHIP and 205 strikeouts across 186 innings. His career numbers are equally strong: a 3.60 ERA, 1.06 WHIP and 1,089 strikeouts over 1,021 1/3 innings.
Pairing Gilbert with Brown would give Houston two legitimate postseason starters and reduce pressure on a rotation ravaged by injuries. The Astros used a franchise-record 18 starters in 2026, and Brown lasted only two-thirds of an inning while allowing four runs in the decisive Wild Card loss.
Seattle would demand a premium for trading an established starter to a division rival. Neyens, Houston's No. 2 prospect, offers significant left-handed power, while Pecko supplies a near-major-league arm and Sullivan adds outfield depth.
That price would hurt a thin farm system, especially with Neyens ranked among MLB's Top 100 prospects. Still, prospects are assets, and Gilbert would address the Astros' most important weakness immediately. Houston should make the trade only with confidence that it can extend him beyond 2027.
Buy low on Jarren Duran
Astros receive: OF Jarren Duran
Red Sox receive: OF Logan Hughes and RHP Bryce Mayer
Duran's value dropped sharply during a disappointing 2026 season, creating a potential buy-low opportunity. He hit .207 with a .266 on-base percentage and .361 slugging percentage, although he still produced 20 home runs and 21 stolen bases in 151 games.
Those numbers are a significant step backward from his 2024 breakout, when he batted .285 with an .834 OPS, 21 homers and 34 steals. His combination of speed, extra-base ability and experience in left and center field would give Houston an element missing from its current lineup.
The risk is obvious. Duran struck out 165 times in 2026 and posted a .627 OPS, so Houston would be betting that a change of scenery and different hitting instruction could revive him. However, he remains under club control for two more seasons, giving the Astros time to recover value.
Boston would receive Houston's No. 3 prospect in Hughes and a pitching prospect in Mayer. Houston would keep its top prospect, Kevin Alvarez, while acquiring an athletic outfielder who could lead off, create pressure on the bases and move around defensively.
Neither trade guarantees another championship, but standing still is the greater danger. Gilbert would stabilize October pitching, while Duran would make the lineup faster and less dependent on home runs. Those are precisely the bold changes Houston needs after another brief postseason appearance.

item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees and Tampa Bay Rays are back at it Monday night for Game 2 of the ALDS at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida, after an off day Sunday. The Yankees dominated Boston in their AL Wild Card Series to advance to the ALDS to face fellow AL East rivals the Rays, but Game 1 on Saturday was far from how New York performed in the previous round.
The Yankees’ lineup ran into Rays All-Star right-hander Drew Rasmussen in Game 1, who carried a no-hitter into the eighth inning before allowing a double to Austin Wells, who ended up getting thrown out at third base to end the inning while trying to stretch it into a triple. Rasmussen finished his outing with eight scoreless innings and 10 strikeouts, with Bryan Baker recording the save and Jonathan Aranda accounting for the only run of the game with his third-inning solo home run in the Rays’ 1-0 shutout victory.
Veteran right-hander Freddy Peralta will look to shut down New York’s lineup Monday night just as Rasmussen did in Game 1. Peralta had a down year overall, but he ended the regular season strong, posting a 4-0 record with a 0.96 ERA and 0.89 WHIP across five starts in September.
Peralta will be going toe-to-toe with likely 2026 American League Cy Young Award winner Cam Schlittler of the Yankees, who’s set to make his second start of this year’s MLB playoffs. The young right-hander owned a 1.95 ERA and 0.92 WHIP and recorded 239 strikeouts during the regular season. He also pitched 6.1 scoreless innings with 10 strikeouts in a win over Boston in the AL Wild Card Series.
See our Yankees vs. Rays MLB playoff predictions, picks, and more below for Monday night’s ALDS Game 2 at Tropicana Field.
Yankees vs. Rays Odds for Game 2
The Rays lead the series 1-0, but the Yankees are listed as road favorites at Hard Rock Bet Sportsbook for Game 2 Monday night with Schlittler and his career 0.87 ERA in the playoffs taking the mound:
Yankees vs. Rays MLB Playoff Predictions
Our Yankees vs. Rays prediction below for Game 2 comes from the Stats Hub at Hard Rock Bet Sportsbook, which offers baseball betting insights and trends, so make sure to check it out while placing wagers:
Rays vs. Yankees Best Bet: Under 0.5 1st Inning Total Runs (-165)
The Stats Hub notes that there has been no run scored during the first inning in each of the Yankees’ last six games. That trend could continue Monday night.
There wasn’t much offense at all in Game 1 between the Yankees and Rays on Saturday. The Yankees were shut out and nearly no-hit, and even though the Rays scored a run in the win, Tampa Bay’s offense totaled only five hits and went 0-for-5 with runners in scoring position.
Now Cam Schlittler is taking the mound for the Yankees in Game 2, and we already mentioned how dominant he was during the regular season, in his first start this postseason, and through his first three career playoff outings. We also mentioned that Freddy Peralta didn’t quite have his best season on the mound, but he ended the regular season on a high note and has allowed only three runs over his last six starts.
Both lineups feature plenty of offensive firepower, but it’s hard to ignore how well these two starting pitchers have been throwing the ball.

item.title: [NBC Sports] 2026 Fantasy baseball league winners: Jacob Misiorowski, Jordan Walker, Miguel Vargas, more
item.dc:creator: Eric Samulski

item.content:encoded:
We’ve had some time for the dust to settle on the 2026 fantasy baseball season, which means it’s time to look back on what we learned (or should have learned) before we turn the page to 2027. I figured I’d start by looking at “league winners.”
We love to throw the term “league winner” around, but what does it really mean? I could have looked at all the teams who won leagues and found the players who appeared on most of them. That would be valid, but I don’t have all that data at my fingertips, and I believe the players who “won” you something were the players who outproduced their acquisition cost by the most. So that’s what I looked at: which players produced the most fantasy value based on what it cost to get them. Which players gave you the biggest return on investment. Chances are, if you hit on one or more of these guys, you were in for a pretty solid season.
To measure what their return on investment was, I took the FanGraphs Player Rater dollar values for 12-team leagues and used the Player Rater’s ADP, which is derived from NFBC formats. I compared what each player earned with what his draft position should have earned. The “should have earned” part, I needed some help with, so I had Claude average the 2026 earnings of every player drafted within a reasonable range (about 22%) of the ADP for that pick. So, for example, if the player was the 100th pick, I looked at the value produced by players drafted 78th through 128th. That felt like a fair way to say, “this pick should have produced a value around this amount.”
I referred to that below as their “Slot Cost.” Every pick after pick 250, I also treated as a waiver wire add, which meant it cost nothing to acquire the player. By taking the final dollar value for each player and subtracting their slot cost, we’re left with the players who earned far more than it cost to draft/acquire them.
So who were those players in 2026?
2026 Fantasy Baseball League-Winning Hitters
| Player | Pos | 2026 ADP | Slot cost | 2026 $ | Profit vs slot |
| Pete Crow-Armstrong | OF | 33 | $14.1 | $49.5 | +$35.5 |
| Jordan Walker | OF | 512 | $0.0 | $29.4 | +$29.4 |
| Ben Rice | C/1B/DH | 53 | $9.7 | $36.6 | +$26.9 |
| Miguel Vargas | 1B/3B | 303 | $0.0 | $26.5 | +$26.5 |
| Otto Lopez | 2B/SS | 229 | $0.0 | $26.5 | +$26.5 |
| CJ Abrams | SS | 65 | $9.1 | $33.9 | +$24.8 |
| Sal Stewart | 1B/3B | 162 | $3.3 | $27.9 | +$24.6 |
| Jake McCarthy | OF | 507 | $0.0 | $24.4 | +$24.4 |
| Gabriel Moreno | C/DH | 181 | $0.4 | $24.2 | +$23.8 |
| Alec Burleson | 1B/OF/DH | 175 | $0.9 | $23.9 | +$23.0 |
Not a ton of surprises here. Even though Pete Crow-Armstrong was a top 40 pick, he still vastly outperformed his draft slot. His production so far has exceeded everyone else’s, so he was the ultimate “league winner.” Ben Rice and CJ Abrams were also early-round picks who returned far more than it cost to acquire them, keeping in mind that Rice is catcher-eligible and this is for two-catcher formats.
PCA, Rice, and Abrams also join a group of hitters here who were already pretty good in 2025. Alec Burleson, Miguel Vargas, and Otto Lopez all had flashed usable production in 2025 and were locked into full-time roles. We may not have seen this jump coming, but we likely could have been drafting them higher based on underlying skills and roles.
We have talked ad nauseuam about Jordan Walker‘s breakout and ways in which we could have seen it coming. Sal Stewart was a highly touted rookie who delivered in his first full season, while both Gabriel Moreno and Jake McCarthy earned far more playing time than they were projected to. Moreno had never had more than 380 plate appearances in a season, but had 550 this year, and McCarthy won a starting job in Colorado, which also made him our staff vote for comeback player of the year.
Some other waiver wire players (ADP after pick 250) who came close to making this list were: Dillon Dingler ($22 value in 2026), Liam Hicks ($22), Jake Bauers ($20.8), Carter Jensen ($18.8), Luis Garcia Jr. ($18.6), Kevin McGonigle ($17.8), Carson Benge ($17.8), and Brooks Lee ($14.1).
2026 Fantasy Baseball League-Winning Pitchers
| Player | Pos | 2026 ADP | Slot cost | 2026 $ | Profit vs slot |
| Jacob Misiorowski | SP | 114 | $6.3 | $41.7 | +$35.4 |
| Cam Schlittler | SP | 117 | $5.2 | $37.6 | +$32.4 |
| Drew Rasmussen | SP | 132 | $4.9 | $28.9 | +$24.0 |
| Parker Messick | SP | 294 | $0.0 | $23.0 | +$23.0 |
| Jacob Latz | SP/RP | 731 | $0.0 | $17.6 | +$17.6 |
| Logan Henderson | SP | 413 | $0.0 | $17.4 | +$17.4 |
| Cade Cavalli | SP | 305 | $0.0 | $16.5 | +$16.5 |
| Nick Martinez | SP | 738 | $0.0 | $16.4 | +$16.4 |
| Dylan Cease | SP | 75 | $7.9 | $23.6 | +$15.7 |
| Yoshinobu Yamamoto | SP | 27 | $15.2 | $30.7 | +$15.6 |
Again, we start the list with names that are not particularly surprising. Jacob Misiorowski and Cam Schlittler were the best two pitchers in the league this season, and neither one of them was drafted inside the top 100 picks. Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Dylan Cease were the only two other semi-highly drafted pitchers who produced a “league-winning” return on your investment. I guess we can include Drew Rasmussen in there too.
Of this group of ten pitchers, five of them (Misiorowski, Schlittler, Logan Henderson, Parker Messick, and Cade Cavalli) were high strikeout rate arms who didn’t pitch enough innings in 2025 to be among the top arms drafted. In fairness to drafters, Parker Messick wasn’t officially in the rotation until the end of May, and Cade Cavalli was fairly mediocre until a pitch mix change and velocity bump in the middle of June. Still, betting on strikeout arms coming off limited workload makes sense.
The majority of the other names on here had a clear role/situation change. Drew Rasmussen was another year removed from injury and went up over 170 innings. Nick Martinez was given a chance to be a full-time starter, Jacob Latz was turned into a closer, and Dylan Cease changed organizations, which led to massive improvement from his changeup and attack plan.
So who could fit this bill in 2027?
Potential League-Winning Hitters in 2027
| Player | Pos | 2026 age | 2026 PA | Barrel % | 2026 $ |
| Heriberto Hernández | OF/DH | 26 | 505 | 12.7 | $4.1 |
| Spencer Torkelson | 1B | 26 | 612 | 12.2 | $6.0 |
| Colson Montgomery | 3B/SS | 24 | 638 | 12 | $7.6 |
| Munetaka Murakami | 1B | 26 | 553 | 20.5 | $9.1 |
| Chase DeLauter | OF/DH | 24 | 559 | 6.3 | $10.5 |
| Jac Caglianone | 1B/OF | 23 | 553 | 13 | $14.2 |
| Riley Greene | OF/DH | 25 | 592 | 14.8 | $14.6 |
| Garrett Mitchell | OF | 27 | 531 | 11.7 | $8.3 |
| Wilyer Abreu | OF | 27 | 681 | 12.5 | $13.2 |
| Luis García Jr. | 1B/2B | 26 | 543 | 12.2 | $18.6 |
If we’re going to identify who were league winners in 2026, then it makes sense to use that information to project who would be a league winner in 2027. The hitters who made the league winner list seemed to fall into two categories: Players who had already shown flashes of success and were underpriced (Rice, Burleson, Vargas, PCA, Lopez) and players who experienced a significant bump in playing time from the previous season (Walker, Stewart, McCarthy, Moreno).
It’s hard to use 2026 numbers to project who will have a playing time boost in 2027, so I’ll leave that part to the side for now. To find potentially underpriced hitters, I wanted to look at the commonalities behind the hitters who were “league winners” this year. Among all qualified hitters, having a 12%+ barrel rate or a 91+ mph average exit velocity, combined with being age 26 or younger, doubled the rate of $10+ profits returned. Meanwhile, strikeout rate, walk rate, chase rate, and swinging-strike rate had no relationship to profit.
That means, if we’re looking for players to break out in 2027, we should be looking for players entering their athletic prime who hit the ball hard. Not a shocking revelation, and I already write an off-season column about hitters entering their athletic prime years. This year, that column mentioned Rice, Vargas, Lopez, Ryan Jeffers, Wilyer Abreu, Alejandro Kirk, and a collection of hitters who did not break out (Brett Baty, Heliot Ramos, Andrew Vaughn, etc.)
In addition to the list above, there are a few players who fit the hard contact and age profile but will likely already be priced up by the market. I’m not going to list them as potential league winners, but they should be targets for you in drafts, even at cost: Walker, Stewart, Vargas, Drake Baldwin, Hunter Goodman, Carter Jensen, James Wood and Jackson Chourio. All earned $18–30 this season and could see a sizeable boost from that in 2027.
Of the others listed, Jac Caglianone might be the best fit based on age and his 13% barrel rate and 93.3 mph average exit velocity. We already know why Riley Greene is an exciting fantasy option, but he produced just $15 of value in 2026. There’s a path for him to be a $30+ guy. Heriberto Hernandez and Chase DeLauter could take big steps forward with more playing time; Luis Garcia Jr. has a full season in Yankee Stadium, and all of Spencer Torkelson, Munetaka Murakami, and Colson Montgomery have the batted ball quality but major contact issues. If they can make strides in their contact rates, their power could lead to a massive return on investment for fantasy.
Potential League-Winning Pitchers in 2027
| Player | Team | Pos | 2026 IP | K/IP | 2026 $ |
| Didier Fuentes | ATL | SP/RP | 73.1 | 1.26 | $9.1 |
| Jonah Tong | NYM | SP | 30.2 | 1.13 | -$3.6 |
| Tatsuya Imai | HOU | SP | 76.2 | 1.27 | -$7.3 |
| Gage Jump | ATH | SP | 98.2 | 1.10 | -$15.4 |
| Brandon Sproat | MIL | SP | 97.0 | 1.04 | -$16.3 |
| Jack Leiter | TEX | SP | 80.0 | 1.04 | -$12.8 |
| Jackson Jobe | DET | SP | 46.0 | 1.11 | -$2.1 |
| Mason Montgomery | PIT | SP/RP | 68.2 | 1.54 | $13.3 |
| Grant Taylor | CHW | SP/RP | 84.0 | 1.26 | $13.8 |
Looking at the starting pitchers who made our “league-winners” list earlier in the article, the key is strikeouts. Among all starters drafted at an ADP between 90–400, those who threw under 100 innings in 2025 and posted a 1.0 K/IP or higher averaged $4.40 or more when compared to their slot, and 31% of them returned $10+ profit. So we need to be looking for starting pitchers like that. The names that came up were Didier Fuentes, Jonah Tong, and Logan Henderson. Of course, Henderson already was a “league-winner” in 2026, so his price will be high.
Younger pitchers who had the strikeouts but a poor ERA also fit the bill. Remember that Misiorowski had a 4.36 ERA in 2025. He was missing tons of bats, but the surface-level ratios weren’t ideal. Pitchers like Tatsuya Imai, Brandon Sproat, Jackson Jobe, and Jack Leiter all fit the bill. So did Gage Jump and Mason Barnett, but factoring in the element of pitching in Sacramento muddies those waters.
The other names on this list, Mason Montgomery and Grant Taylor, are either elite closers or potentially breakout starters if they’re moved back into the rotation. There is obviously a lot of uncertainty with their roles in 2027, but they are names to keep an eye on, especially if we have a better idea of their role.

item.content:encoded:
Ranking Every MLB Playoff Team's Projected 2026 Postseason Rotation
Pitching wins championships.
While that old adage still holds true, it has taken on a slightly different meaning in today's game, as teams need to successfully utilize their entire pitching staff to make a deep playoff run, rather than simply leaning on two or three starting pitchers to shoulder the load.
Still, a strong performance from the starting staff can give a team a major leg up. The Los Angeles Dodgers were the perfect example of that last October.
Ahead, we've ranked the playoff rotations of every postseason team. Which team's rotation is best positioned heading into the playoffs?
12. Houston Astros
1 of 12
RHP Hunter Brown (6-3, 3.26 ERA, 1.28 WHIP, 120 K, 102.0 IP)
RHP Hayden Wesneski (5-2, 3.50 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 41 K, 54.0 IP)
RHP Peter Lambert (8-10, 3.87 ERA, 1.26 WHIP, 153 K, 153.2 IP)
RHP Ethan Pecko (1-0, 4.31 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 21 K, 31.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Ronel Blanco, RHP Cristian Javier (out for ALWC)
The Astros have used 19 different starting pitchers this year while navigating a long list of injuries. The fact that reliever AJ Blubaugh ranks third on the team with 95.1 innings pitched speaks volumes.
Ace Hunter Brown was slowed by a shoulder strain in the first half of the season, but he has returned to form with a 3.11 ERA and 81 strikeouts in 66.2 innings since the All-Star break.
With Cristian Javier making an early exit from his start on Wednesday, the rotation behind Brown is entirely up in the air. Hayden Wesneski and Peter Lambert are both capable of tossing a quality start, but they are short on big-game experience and could also be susceptible to a quick hook, shifting the focus to a Houston bullpen that ranks 17th in the majors with a 4.09 ERA.
11. Chicago White Sox
2 of 12
RHP Sean Burke (10-7, 3.40 ERA, 1.20 WHIP, 178 K, 167.0 IP)
RHP Davis Martin (9-7, 3.84 ERA, 1.29 WHIP, 121 K, 145.1 IP)
RHP Erick Fedde (8-9, 3.83 ERA, 1.36 WHIP, 99 K, 141.0 IP)
LHP Anthony Kay (9-9, 4.53 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 125 K, 153.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Luis Castillo, RHP David Sandlin
The White Sox rank 26th in starters' ERA (4.62) and 28th in quality starts (34), so the starting rotation is something they will need to figure out how to navigate in the postseason rather than a strength.
Sean Burke and Davis Martin have accounted for 21 of those 33 quality starts. They will be asked to chew up innings at the top of the rotation, while games outside of their starts will likely be an all-hands-on-deck situation.
Sean Newcomb (58 G, 6 GS, 3.17 ERA, 88.0 IP) and Grant Taylor (59 G, 4 GS, 2.30 ERA, 82.0 IP) are both capable of providing length out of the bullpen, while deadline pickup Luis Castillo has also been shifted to a relief role.
10. Chicago Cubs
3 of 12
LHP Shota Imanaga (11-10, 3.74 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 173.1 IP)
RHP Kevin Gausman (4-2, 4.83 ERA, 1.23 WHIP, 57 K, 50.1 IP)
LHP Matthew Boyd (10-5, 3.91 ERA, 1.21 WHIP, 96 K, 126.2 IP)
LHP David Peterson (6-2, 3.94 ERA, 1.39 WHIP, 68 K, 75.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Clay Holmes, RHP Javier Assad
The Cubs roll into October with arguably the best offense and best defense in baseball, but questions about their pitching staff hang over their postseason outlook.
Shota Imanaga has a 1.96 ERA and a 23-to-2 strikeout-to-walk ratio over 23 innings in September. That should put him in line to be the ace of the staff in October.
Veteran Kevin Gausman's significant playoff experience, including starting Game 2 and Game 6 of the World Series a year ago, should earn him a prominent role in the playoffs. At the back of the staff, Clay Holmes is the obvious candidate to shift to the bullpen given his past experience closing games.
9. San Diego Padres
4 of 12
RHP Michael King (12-10, 3.21 ERA, 1.18 WHIP, 159 K, 185.0 IP)
RHP Nick Pivetta (3-2, 2.86 ERA, 1.01 WHIP, 42 K, 34.2 IP)
RHP Walker Buehler (9-6, 4.56 ERA, 1.34 WHIP, 128 K, 150.0 IP)
LHP Robbie Ray (3-2, 5.02 ERA, 1.54 WHIP, 33 K, 43.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Casey Mize, RHP Randy Vásquez
The Padres rank fourth in the majors and top among projected playoff teams with 666.0 innings of work from their bullpen. That relief corps, anchored by Mason Miller and Adrian Morejón, will be a major factor in October.
Michael King is the clear ace of the staff. Nick Pivetta has pitched well since returning on Sept. 7, with 11 hits and three earned runs allowed in 14 innings over three starts.
Behind them, Walker Buehler is the logical Game 3 candidate, given his postseason resume and 3.15 ERA over 45.2 innings in his last nine starts. Deadline pickups Robbie Ray and Casey Mize have struggled since coming to San Diego and could be X-factors if they advance beyond the Wild Card Round.
8. Cleveland Guardians
5 of 12
RHP Gavin Williams (14-8, 3.63 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 244 K, 181.0 IP)
LHP Parker Messick (12-9, 2.55 ERA, 1.04 WHIP, 191 K, 183.1 IP)
RHP Tanner Bibee (6-15, 4.35 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 142 K, 182.0 IP)
LHP Joey Cantillo (11-9, 3.62 ERA, 1.42 WHIP, 171 K, 159.0 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Foster Griffin
Gavin Williams leads the AL with 244 strikeouts and Parker Messick has a 2.27 ERA in 71.1 innings since the All-Star break, giving the Guardians a legitimate one-two punch to lead the way in the postseason.
Opening Day starter Tanner Bibee has struggled, posting an 8.24 ERA over 19.2 innings in September, but his track record still makes him the most likely candidate to start Game 3.
The question then becomes who gets the nod between Foster Griffin and Joey Cantillo. Griffin has a 5.19 ERA in nine starts since he was acquired at the trade deadline, while Cantillo has better surface-level results but has issued an AL-leading 81 walks in 159 innings.
7. Atlanta Braves
6 of 12
LHP Chris Sale (14-9, 2.16 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 200 K, 162.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Mahle (4-1, 1.99 ERA, 0.96 WHIP, 48 K, 54.1 IP)
RHP Grant Holmes (10-5, 3.47 ERA, 1.30 WHIP, 114 K, 147.2 IP)
RHP JR Ritchie (1-4, 4.79 ERA, 1.46 WHIP, 66 K, 67.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Bryce Elder, RHP AJ Smith-Shawver, LHP Martín Pérez (out for NLWC)
Starting pitching was expected to be a glaring issue for the Braves when Spencer Strider, Spencer Schwellenbach, Hurston Waldrep and AJ Smith-Shawver all began the season on the injured list.
Instead, Chris Sale has put together a Cy Young-caliber season, while journeyman veterans Martín Pérez and Grant Holmes have combined for a 3.26 ERA in 289.2 innings spanning 55 starts. However, Pérez was just placed on the injured list with lower back inflammation, making a bullpen game the likely approach to fill the fourth starter role if they advance to the NLDS.
Deadline pickup Tyler Mahle has given them the No. 2 starter they still lacked, while a healthy Bryce Elder could be an X-factor if they advance deeper into October.
6. Milwaukee Brewers
7 of 12
RHP Jacob Misiorowski (15-5, 1.86 ERA, 0.80 WHIP, 247 K, 169.1 IP)
RHP Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47 ERA, 0.84 WHIP, 110 K, 98.1 IP)
LHP Robert Gasser (5-5, 4.01 ERA, 1.24 WHIP, 94 K, 103.1 IP)
RHP Dustin May (2-2, 5.61 ERA, 1.43 WHIP, 33 K, 33.2 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Kyle Harrison, LHP Shane Drohan
Jacob Misiorowski pitched out of the bullpen for the Brewers last October, posting a 1.50 ERA, 0.83 WHIP and 16 strikeouts in 12 innings across three appearances. He is now poised to lead their staff this postseason.
Rookie Logan Henderson has not allowed more than three earned runs in any of his 18 starts this season. He is 8-2 with a 2.19 ERA and 0.79 WHIP in 70 innings since the All-Star break.
Left-hander Robert Gasser has a 1.71 ERA in 26.1 innings over his last five appearances. He will be a significant part of manager Pat Murphy's plan of mixing and matching innings behind Misiorowski and Henderson.
5. Boston Red Sox
8 of 12
RHP Sonny Gray (18-5, 2.72 ERA, 1.15 WHIP, 149 K, 169.0 IP)
LHP Ranger Suarez (8-5, 3.22 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 140 K, 148.1 IP)
LHP Payton Tolle (9-6, 3.03 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 171 K, 148.2 IP)
RHP Brayan Bello (6-7, 4.49 ERA, 1.37 WHIP, 90 K, 112.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Jake Bennett, LHP Patrick Sandoval
Few offseason additions have made a bigger impact than Sonny Gray, who has 20 quality starts in 29 games this year and is on track for his fourth career top-10 finish in Cy Young voting for four different teams.
Rookie Payton Tolle has been the team's most consistent starter behind Gray this year and will factor into the playoff rotation, while high-priced offseason signing Ranger Suarez has a 1.09 ERA over 24.2 innings in September.
The X-factor could be Brayan Bello after he threw a gem (8.0 IP, 5 H, 1 ER, 11 K) on the road against the Rays on Sept. 19. He has a 2.28 ERA over 51.1 innings while working mostly out of the bullpen since returning from a minor league demotion before the All-Star break, but he is stretched back out to start.
4. Tampa Bay Rays
9 of 12
RHP Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA, 0.91 WHIP, 174 K, 172.0 IP)
RHP Nick Martinez (15-5, 2.94 ERA, 1.07 WHIP, 108 K, 177.1 IP)
RHP Freddy Peralta (4-2, 3.60 ERA, 0.98 WHIP, 39 K, 50.0 IP)
RHP Griffin Jax (8-10, 3.62 ERA, 1.19 WHIP, 115 K, 109.1 IP)
Other Candidates: LHP Ian Seymour, LHP Shane McClanahan (out for ALDS)
Few organizations do a better job fully utilizing the entire pitching staff than the Rays, but this October they have three legitimate rotation anchors who can get them deep into games in Drew Rasmussen, Nick Martinez and deadline pickup Freddy Peralta.
That group gets even deeper if Shane McClanahan returns to action, though he has already been ruled out for the ALDS. Even if he's not able to return, reliever-turned-starter Griffin Jax has also been quietly excellent this season with a 3.23 ERA and 105 strikeouts in 100.1 innings over his 22 starts.
They could still opt to utilize an opener when it makes sense, or piggyback one of their starters with left-hander Ian Seymour if the situation arises. This isn't a staff that needs to lean on multiple bullpen games to get through a series.
3. Philadelphia Phillies
10 of 12
LHP Cristopher Sánchez (18-6, 2.93 ERA, 1.22 WHIP, 221 K, 200.0 IP)
RHP Zack Wheeler (13-5, 3.06 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 188 K, 156.0 IP)
RHP Aaron Nola (7-11, 4.54 ERA, 1.33 WHIP, 177 K, 174.1 IP)
LHP Jesús Luzardo (14-5, 2.87 ERA, 1.08 WHIP, 221 K, 178.2 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Andrew Painter
Jesús Luzardo played catch earlier this week as he works his way back from shoulder inflammation, though his postseason status remains up in the air. There's a chance he will be limited to bullpen work early in the playoffs.
Veteran Aaron Nola has hit his stride of late, posting a 2.45 ERA in 66 innings over his last 11 starts, so he can fill the void behind the dynamic one-two punch of Cristopher Sánchez (7.7 WAR, 1st among all SP) and Zack Wheeler (5.6 WAR, 8th among all SP).
The Phillies rank second in the majors with 73 quality starts and 869.1 innings from their starting staff, so they are poised to lean on their starters as hard as anyone in October.
2. New York Yankees
11 of 12
RHP Cam Schlittler (14-6, 1.95 ERA, 0.92 WHIP, 239 K, 193.2 IP)
LHP Max Fried (5-5, 2.80 ERA, 0.99 WHIP, 104 K, 112.2 IP)
RHP Gerrit Cole (10-9, 3.61 ERA, 1.10 WHIP, 131 K, 127.0 IP)
LHP Carlos Rodón (7-3, 2.67 ERA, 1.06 WHIP, 91 K, 84.1 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Will Warren
With AL Cy Young favorite Cam Schlittler and three established veteran starters capable of frontline production in Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón, the Yankees rotation is capable of making a major impact in October.
Schlittler logged a 1.26 ERA over 14.1 innings last October, including eight scoreless frames against the rival Red Sox in the Wild Card Round. He will now be asked to shoulder a heavier load.
It remains to be seen who the odd-man out would be in a series that calls for a three-man staff, though Rodón has made his case with a 1.42 ERA, 0.75 WHIP and 28 strikeouts in 25.1 innings in September.
1. Los Angeles Dodgers
12 of 12
RHP Yoshinobu Yamamoto (14-9, 2.53 ERA, 0.87 WHIP, 182 K, 185.0 IP)
LHP Tarik Skubal (4-2, 2.95 ERA, 1.13 WHIP, 60 K, 55.0 IP)
LHP Blake Snell (4-1, 1.86 ERA, 1.09 WHIP, 52 K, 38.2 IP)
RHP Tyler Glasnow (5-2, 3.53 ERA, 0.95 WHIP, 98 K, 74.0 IP)
Other Candidates: RHP Emmet Sheehan, LHP Justin Wrobleski
The Dodgers have once again navigated much of the regular season without Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, but they are healthy rolling into October and poised to round out the playoff rotation alongside Yoshinobu Yamamoto and deadline pickup Tarik Skubal.
The starting rotation logged a 2.68 ERA over 104 innings last postseason, with Yamamoto, Snell and Glasnow starting 13 of 17 games and the rest going to Shohei Ohtani, who will be limited to DH duties but has been sufficiently replaced by a two-time Cy Young winner in Skubal.
Right-hander Emmet Sheehan has a 0.53 ERA and 24 strikeouts over 17 innings in three September starts. He will serve as a multi-inning weapon out of the bullpen.

item.dc:creator: Matt Larter

item.content:encoded:
The MLB postseason has seen New York Yankees ace Cam Schlittler accomplish a feat that has not been matched in 90 years.
Cam Schlittler has 24 strikeouts and 1 walk allowed through 3 career postseason starts.The only other pitcher with 20 or more Ks and no more than 1 walk through his first 3 playoff starts all-time is Schoolboy Rowe (20 K, 0 BB) in 1934-1935. https://t.co/F3FfMIHHBg
— OptaSTATS (@OptaSTATS) October 5, 2026
Schlittler has recorded 24 strikeouts and just one walk through his first three career playoff starts, putting him in incredibly rare company.
The only other pitcher in MLB history to record at least 20 strikeouts while allowing no more than one walk through his first three postseason starts was Schoolboy Rowe of the Detroit Tigers, who struck out 20 and walked none between 1934 and 1935.
Schlittler dominates in postseason
Jul 29, 2026; Chicago, Illinois, USA; New York Yankees starting pitcher Cam Schlittler (31) walks back to the dugout during the sixth inning of a baseball game against the Chicago White Sox at Rate Field. Mandatory Credit: Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
Schlittler's latest performance came against the Boston Red Sox in the opening game of the American League Wild Card Series. The right-hander delivered 6.1 scoreless innings while striking out 10 batters, leading the Yankees to a commanding 9-0 victory.
New York went on to sweep Boston in two games, with Schlittler playing a major role in helping the Yankees advance.
The 25-year-old sophomore has been one of the most dominant pitchers in baseball throughout the 2026 season. During the regular season, Schlittler posted a 14-6 record with a remarkable 1.95 ERA and 0.92 WHIP across 33 appearances. He also recorded an impressive 239 strikeouts.
Those numbers have made Schlittler one of the leading candidates for the American League Cy Young Award.
Yankees turn to Schlittler again
Schlittler's dominance has carried over into October. Through his first three career postseason appearances, he now owns a 0.87 ERA and a microscopic 0.77 WHIP.
The Yankees will need another strong performance from their young ace after dropping Game 1 of the American League Division Series to the Tampa Bay Rays. New York suffered a narrow 1-0 defeat against the division-winning Rays, putting additional pressure on the Yankees heading into Game 2.
Schlittler is expected to take the mound Monday, giving New York a chance to even the series with its most reliable postseason weapon.
With his combination of strikeout ability, control and run prevention, Schlittler has already etched his name alongside a pitcher from nine decades ago. Another dominant outing could further cement his status as one of the Yankees' emerging postseason stars.

item.title: [heavy.com] Braves Predicted to Part Ways With Spencer Strider
item.dc:creator: Billy Heyen
item.description: Spencer Strider seemed at one point like he might develop into the best pitcher in all of Major League Baseball. Those days are gone, though. The Atlanta Braves don’t have Strider available to them as they compete in the 2026 postseason. And at least some are beginning to wonder whether Strider will ever pitch for the Braves again. item.content:encoded:
Spencer Strider seemed at one point like he might develop into the best pitcher in all of Major League Baseball.
Those days are gone, though. The Atlanta Braves don’t have Strider available to them as they compete in the 2026 postseason.
And at least some are beginning to wonder whether Strider will ever pitch for the Braves again.
Spencer Strider Trade Prediction
In a new article by Bleacher Report’s Kerry Miller, it’s predicted that Strider won’t play for the Braves in 2027. Instead, this prediction says that Strider will get moved this offseason in a trade.
The predicted trade would send Strider to the Baltimore Orioles.
In return, the Orioles would trade the Braves shortstop prospect Wehiwa Aloy and outfield prospect Nate George.
Miller notes that it was suggested that the Braves might’ve traded Strider to the Rangers for Jacob deGrom over the summer.
That didn’t happen, but it could point to Strider’s days being numbered.
“Baltimore could be a great fit, especially if Atlanta is willing to retain some of the (at least) $49M still due to Strider,” Miller writes. “At the moment, the Orioles’ starting rotation for 2027 looks like Shane Baz, Kyle Bradish, Brandon Young and some serious question marks. And with Chris Bassitt, Zach Eflin, Andrew Kittredge and more coming off the books, they should have room in the budget to take a gamble on Strider. At any rate, they’re going to have to invest in pitching, unless they’re irrationally confident in two of Cade Povich, Trey Gibson and Luis De León making an impact in 2027. Why not Strider if they can get him?”
Of the prospects, Aloy has some serious believers. Shortstop isn’t a position the Braves have a ton of clear standouts rising toward, and Aloy could climb into an MLB contributor if he kept developing.
Why Braves Would Trade Spencer Strider
Strider simply hasn’t been able to stay healthy.
An injured Strider isn’t worth much to Atlanta, especially considering his contract isn’t cheap.
“When he was healthy, Strider was all sorts of special, arguably the best pitcher in all of baseball between the 2022 and 2023 campaigns,” Miller writes. “There were also flashes of his former dominance during the 2025 season, making 11 quality starts. But he missed almost all of 2024 and most of 2026 to injuries and might never get back to what he used to be. Could the Braves revisit that attempt to get out from under the remainder of this contract? And is anyone willing to help them do so?”
It would be a sad day in Atlanta if they moved on from Strider, but the sport doesn’t wait up for those who are lagging behind.
If the Braves don’t believe Strider can be what he once was, then trading him away might be the best path to moving forward. They’d just need a suitor willing to give them a reasonable return.
